expected_concepts: Briefly review vectors as directed line segments. Introduce the concept of 'projection' visually: imagine casting a shadow of vector A onto the axis of vector B. Establish that the length of this shadow depends on the angle between them. This sets the stage for the geometric interpretation of the dot product.

Define the dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}| |\mathbf{b}| \cos \theta$. Explain that it is a scalar value representing the 'alignment' of two vectors. Emphasize that it measures how much of vector A lies in the direction of vector B. Highlight the critical cases: 90 degrees (orthogonal) results in 0, and 0 degrees (parallel) results in the product of magnitudes.

Transition from geometric intuition to algebraic computation. Show that the geometric formula is equivalent to the sum of component-wise products ($x_1x_2 + y_1y_2$). Explain that this algebraic form allows us to calculate alignment without needing to know the angle explicitly, making it computationally powerful for machines and algorithms.

Introduce the core concept of duality. In a finite-dimensional space, every vector $\mathbf{v}$ can be viewed not just as an arrow, but as a linear function (a functional) that takes another vector $\mathbf{w}$ and returns a scalar. This function is precisely the dot product with $\mathbf{v}$: $f_{\mathbf{v}}(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{w}$. Explain that the 'dual space' consists of these functions.

Apply the duality concept to a practical scenario. If the dot product is zero, the vectors are orthogonal (uncorrelated). In signal processing, this means a signal (vector A) has no component in the direction of a noise filter (vector B). Use this to explain how we can 'detect' features by projecting data onto basis vectors (dual basis).

Define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] as ad - bc. Visually demonstrate that this value equals the signed area of the parallelogram formed by the transformed basis vectors. Highlight that if the determinant is 1, area is preserved; if >1, area expands; if <1, area shrinks. Explain the sign indicates orientation (clockwise vs. counter-clockwise).

expected_concepts: Introduce the concept that a vector is an abstract entity, but its coordinates depend on the 'language' (basis) used to describe it. Visualize the standard basis vectors i and j as the axes of a 2D grid. Explain that changing the basis is like switching from describing a location using 'East/North' to 'Up-Left/Down-Right'.

Explain how to define a new basis using two linearly independent vectors, B1 and B2. Visually show these new vectors replacing the original i and j axes. Emphasize that the new basis vectors form the columns of the change-of-basis matrix. Highlight that the origin remains fixed, but the grid lines rotate/skew.

Construct the matrix P by placing the new basis vectors B1 and B2 as columns. Explain that P transforms coordinates from the new basis to the standard basis. Show the matrix multiplication visually: [B1 B2] * [coords_in_new_basis] = [coords_in_standard_basis]. Use color-coding to link the columns of P to the vectors B1 and B2.

Demonstrate how to find the coordinates of a vector V in the new basis. Explain that we need to 'undo' the transformation of P, so we use the inverse matrix P⁻¹. Show the equation: coords_new = P⁻¹ * coords_standard. Animate the process: start with V in standard basis, apply P⁻¹ to get V in the new basis. Emphasize that P⁻¹ exists only if the basis vectors are linearly independent (non-parallel).

Show a practical application where changing basis simplifies a problem. For example, diagonalizing a matrix to decouple equations, or aligning coordinates with principal axes of a shape. Visualize a skewed ellipse becoming a circle when the basis is aligned with its axes. Conclude that change of basis is a powerful tool for simplifying analysis, not just a coordinate swap.

sections.title: The Coordinate System as a Language
sections.content: Introduce the concept that a vector is an abstract entity, but its coordinates depend on the 'language' (basis) used to describe it. Visualize the standard basis vectors i and j as the axes of a 2D grid. Explain that changing the basis is like switching from describing a location using 'East/North' to 'Up-Left/Down-Right'.
sections.example: A robot arm in a warehouse. In the global frame, the arm is at (3, 4). If the robot's local frame is rotated, the arm's position relative to the robot changes, even though the physical arm hasn't moved.

sections.title: Defining the New Basis
sections.content: Explain how to define a new basis using two linearly independent vectors, B1 and B2. Visually show these new vectors replacing the original i and j axes. Emphasize that the new basis vectors form the columns of the change-of-basis matrix. Highlight that the origin remains fixed, but the grid lines rotate/skew.
sections.example: Imagine a map where the axes are aligned with a river (B1) and a road (B2) instead of North and East. The 'grid' of the map now follows the landscape features.

sections.title: The Change-of-Basis Matrix (P)
sections.content: Construct the matrix P by placing the new basis vectors B1 and B2 as columns. Explain that P transforms coordinates from the new basis to the standard basis. sections.example: If B1 = (1, 1) and B2 = (-1, 1), the matrix P is [[1, -1], [1, 1]]. A vector with coordinates (1, 0) in the new basis maps to (1, 1) in the standard basis. Visualize this as scaling and rotating the unit vector of the new basis.

sections.title: Transforming Coordinates: From Old to New
sections.content: Demonstrate how to find the coordinates of a vector V in the new basis. Explain that we need to 'undo' the transformation of P, so we use the inverse matrix P⁻¹. Show the equation: coords_new = P⁻¹ * coords_standard. Animate the process: start with V in standard basis, apply P⁻¹ to get V in the new basis. Emphasize that P⁻¹ exists only if the basis vectors are linearly independent (non-parallel).
sections.example: A character in a video game. The world coordinates are (5, 3). The character's local frame is rotated 45 degrees. To find where the character sees the object, we apply the inverse rotation matrix to the world coordinates.

sections.title: Application: Simplifying Complex Systems
sections.content: Show a practical application where changing basis simplifies a problem. For example, diagonalizing a matrix to decouple equations, or aligning coordinates with principal axes of a shape. Visualize a skewed ellipse becoming a circle when the basis is aligned with its axes. Conclude that change of basis is a powerful tool for simplifying analysis, not just a coordinate swap.
sections.example: Analyzing the vibration of a guitar string. By changing to a basis of normal modes, the complex coupled motion simplifies into independent oscillations, making the physics much easier to solve.
